intro: Light and paint change how an ordinary activity is recorded. Notice where solid shapes, broken spots of color or a sustained narrative put you in relation to the people.
alt: Microsoft works at a desk, stands in patterned shade, meets people on a road and pauses in a quiet kitchen.

variants.name: American Realism
variants.look: Specific posture, furniture and working light locate the figure at a recognizable desk.
variants.history: American realism takes many forms. Late nineteenth-century painter Thomas Eakins brought close study of anatomy and contemporary subjects into his work.
variants.when: Study it when you need a precise account of ordinary posture or a familiar working place.
variants.why: Distinctive tools and gestures show what a person is doing without relying on explanation.

variants.name: Macchiaioli
variants.look: Broad patches of sun and shadow meet sharply under the shelter.
variants.history: The Macchiaioli were painters from nineteenth-century Italy who gathered in Florence. They used distinct contrasting patches, or macchie, to build scenes.
variants.when: Study these patches when trying to simplify a visually complicated view into distinct lights and darks.
variants.why: The larger masses do much of the work of describing form and distance.

variants.name: Peredvizhniki
variants.look: Figures and weathered land form a clear social scene. Body language does as much as the setting to tell the story.
variants.history: The Peredvizhniki, also called the Wanderers, organized traveling exhibitions in the late Russian Empire. Their artists pursued varied approaches to landscape, social life and history.
variants.when: Study it when particular people and circumstances need to tell a legible story together.
variants.why: The readable scene leaves room for a viewer to think about the people and conditions it depicts.

variants.name: Naturalism
variants.look: Subdued light and carefully observed objects give the kitchen an ordinary time of day and a sensible scale.
variants.history: Naturalism is a broad label for close observation. Late nineteenth-century French naturalists such as Jules Bastien-Lepage applied it to ordinary people and settings.
variants.when: Study it when the surface, mood and small particulars of a real place need to stay convincing.
variants.why: Even and consistent observation makes a quiet social scene feel inhabited.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: American Realism: woman at a working desk by high-window glare, poised anatomy and direct detail; Macchiaioli: strong patchwork of large dark shade and warm sunlight under outdoor arbor, no smooth gradients; Peredvizhniki: measured narrative composition of woman in dark dress among workers on a road, weathered textures and earthy light; Naturalism: ordinary standing kitchen scene represented with considered close observation, convincing objects, overcast light and understated palette. Modern office woman as recurring focal character. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
